Orthotropic, homogeneous properties of the composite were computed using classical laminate theory (CLT). Symmetry boundary conditions were used to reduce the model size to one lobe from the full model size of 2 lobes. Furthermore, half of one lobe was modeled, with symmetry boundary conditions applied to the truncated face. An internal pressure of 13.5 bar was applied. Stresses in most of the tank is well below 130 MPa. At the location of the corner, the stresses are higher. This is well below the failure limit for this material (computed via an in-house classical laminate theory (CLT) code to be at 428 MPa) for the quasi-isotropic layup. The corner location with the highest stress was modeled without any structural material in the gap/cavity. Carbon-fiber based ‘noodle’ structural support will be added to the model to reduce stresses. Once this is incorporated in the model, the highest stresses, which are currently well below the allowable limit, are expected to come down further. This suggests that the thickness of the tank can be comfortably reduced. The level of reduction is a topic for detailed design (to have been done in Phase 2 of the program). 2.3. Cylindrical (Phase 1) composite tank Outer Tank Buckling Analysis: Having shown feasibility of the above design, a tank design with cylindrical shape and with hemispherical ends was created for Phase 1 tasks. This was to incorporate some of the technical risks in Phase 1. The design of this tank was described earlier. A detailed structural analysis of the outer and inner tanks was performed. A finite element (FE) of the outer tank (Phase 1 design) was created in Abaqus to analyze the tank for buckling. Initial design considerations pointed us to using a composite-foam sandwich structure. However, for ease of manufacture, it was decided to pursue an all-composite outer tank for Phase 1. First, an eigenvalue analysis of the outer tank was performed- to determine its capacity to buckle under atmospheric pressure. The tank geometry is shown in Figure 7 (a). The material model used was that of a homogenous laminate, with quasi-isotropic properties of a carbon-epoxy system. Ply level properties were taken from literature [1] for a system similar to IMS65-Q183, since material properties for this material were not available at this time. Laminate-level homogenized (quasi-isotropic) properties were computed using Classical Laminate Theory. The eigen-buckling analysis of the outer tank gave the first eigenvalue as 11.7, under a loading of 1.01e5 Pa (1 atm). This suggests that the load required to buckle the tank is 11.7 times the atmospheric pressure. The mode of buckling is at the center of the tank (Figure 7 (b)), as expected. This is the cylindrical portion and is easier to buckle than at the hemispherical ends. This analysis was followed by a Riks analysis of the tank where the atmospheric load was applied explicitly, and the buckling load was computed.
